title: Working with Files (Advanced)
description: Advanced: save text to files, read it back, add to it and handle files that don't exist.

subLevels.title: Writing and reading files
subLevels.summary: Save text in a file and read it back.

blocks.text: Variables disappear when a program ends. A file keeps text so the program can read it again. Working with a file has three steps: open it, read or write, then close it.

blocks.code:
file = open("notes.txt", "w")
file.write("Buy milk")
file.close()
print("Saved!")
explanation: open("notes.txt", "w") opens the file for writing and creates it if needed.
write() puts text into the file; close() finishes and saves it.

blocks.title: In the app
blocks.text: In the Practical tab, files live in the app's private scratch folder, which is emptied when each run ends. Write and read a file in the same program. Use simple names like notes.txt; other folders on your phone are blocked.
write() does not start a new line by itself. "\n" inside a string means "new line".

blocks.code:
file = open("shopping.txt", "w")
file.write("milk\n")
file.write("bread\n")
file.close()

file = open("shopping.txt", "r")
print(file.read())
file.close()
explanation: read() gives back all the text in the file as one string.

items: "w": write. Creates the file, or empties it if it exists.
"r": read. This is the default, so open("shopping.txt") also reads.

blocks.code:
file = open("score.txt", "w")
file.write("10")
file.close()
file = open("score.txt", "w")
file.write("25")
file.close()
file = open("score.txt")
print(file.read())
file.close()
explanation: Opening with "w" again wiped the 10 before 25 was written.

blocks.text: Opening a file with "w" deletes what was in it.
Files store text only. Turn numbers into text with str() before writing, and back with int() after reading.

blocks.code:
file = open("score.txt", "w")
file.write(str(42))
file.close()
file = open("score.txt")
score = int(file.read())
file.close()
print(score + 8)

blocks.text: Passing a number straight to write() fails, because write() only accepts strings.

blocks.output: TypeError: write() argument must be str, not int
blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Writing a number directly: file.write(42) is a TypeError, because files store text. Write str(42) or an f-string, and use int() on the text after reading.

questions.explanation: The file is written with Hi and closed, then opened again and read.
questions.code:
f = open("a.txt", "w")
f.write("Hi")
f.close()
f = open("a.txt", "r")
print(f.read())
f.close()
questions.hint: Follow the text from write() into the file and then back out with read().
optionFeedback: read() returns what is inside the file, not its name.
Right: read() gives back what was written.
"w" is the mode used to open the file; it is not written into it.
close() saves the text, so the file holds Hi when it is read.

questions.explanation: The second open(..., "w") empties the file, so only two is left.
questions.code:
f = open("n.txt", "w")
f.write("one")
f.close()
f = open("n.txt", "w")
f.write("two")
f.close()
f = open("n.txt")
print(f.read())
f.close()
questions.hint: Think about what happens to old text when a file is opened with this mode again.
optionFeedback: Opening with "w" again removes the old text, so one is gone.
Right: "w" wiped one before two was written.
"w" doesn't keep old text, so nothing is joined together.
Nothing adds a new line, and "w" removed one anyway.

questions.prompt: What does mode "w" do if the file already exists?
options: Adds the new text to the end
Empties it and starts writing from the beginning
questions.explanation: "w" always starts with an empty file. The old contents are lost.
questions.hint: Remember what happened to the score of 10 in the lesson.
optionFeedback: "w" never keeps the old text; it starts the file again.
"w" works on files that exist and creates files that don't.
Right: the old text is wiped.
Reading is "r"; "w" is for writing.

options: The file must be opened with "r"
100 is too big to store in a file
write() only accepts text, so use str(100)
questions.explanation: Files store text. write(100) passes an int, which is a TypeError.
questions.hint: Think about what kind of value write() expects to receive.
optionFeedback: "r" is for reading; writing needs "w".
The size isn't the problem; the type is.
close() comes last; after it, you can't write any more.
Right: convert the number to text first.

questions.prompt: What goes in the blank to open log.txt for writing?
questions.explanation: The mode is a short string: "w" for write.
questions.hint: The mode is a single letter, written as a string.
optionFeedback: Right: "w" opens the file for writing.
"r" opens for reading, and write() would fail.
The mode is one letter, not the whole word.
Without quotes, w is a variable name that doesn't exist.

questions.explanation: read() always gives back text, so text is "5", and "5" + "5" joins them: 55.
questions.code:
f = open("n.txt", "w")
f.write("5")
f.close()
f = open("n.txt")
text = f.read()
f.close()
print(text + "5")
questions.hint: Ask what type of value read() gives back, even when it looks like a number.
optionFeedback: Right: two strings are joined.
read() gives back text, so + joins instead of adding.
Both parts are strings, so both appear in the result.
text and "5" are both strings, and + can join two strings.

subLevels.title: with, append and lines
subLevels.summary: Close files automatically, add to files and read them line by line.

blocks.text: with opens a file for the indented block and closes it automatically when the block ends.

blocks.code:
with open("diary.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Day 1: learned files\n")

with open("diary.txt") as file:
    print(file.read())
explanation: as file gives the open file a name.
No close() needed: the block ending closes it.

blocks.text: Prefer with: the file is always closed for you, even if an error happens inside the block.

blocks.code:
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("start\n")
with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("more\n")
    f.write("end\n")
with open("log.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

with open("names.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Asha\nRavi\nMeera\n")

with open("names.txt") as f:
    first = f.readline()
    print(first.strip())
    for line in f:
        print("-", line.strip())
explanation: readline() reads one line, including its \n at the end.
A for loop over a file gives one line at a time and continues where readline() stopped.

blocks.code:
with open("marks.txt", "w") as f:
    for mark in [72, 95, 48]:
        f.write(f"{mark}\n")

total = 0
with open("marks.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        total += int(line.strip())
print("Total:", total)

with open("pets.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("cat\ndog\n")
with open("pets.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line)

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Forgetting that every line ends with \n. print(line) then adds a second new line, so you get blank lines. Use line.strip().

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Lines from a file are always text. Use int() or float() to do maths with them.

questions.explanation: "a" adds to the end of the file, so B goes after A.
questions.code:
with open("t.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("A")
with open("t.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("B")
with open("t.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
questions.hint: Compare what the second mode does to existing text with what the first mode does.
optionFeedback: "a" doesn't wipe the file; that is what "w" does.
"a" adds B to the end instead of ignoring it.
Right: append keeps A and adds B.
write() adds no new line by itself, so A and B sit side by side.

questions.prompt: What does with do when its indented block ends?
options: Opens the file a second time
questions.explanation: with closes the file for you when the block finishes.
questions.hint: Think about which step you no longer need to write yourself when using with.
optionFeedback: Right: no close() needed.
The file is opened once, at the start of the with block.
The mode decides reading or writing; with doesn't change it.
The file and its text stay; with only closes it.

questions.explanation: The first readline() reads red. The second readline() reads the next line, green.
questions.code:
with open("c.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("red\ngreen\nblue\n")
with open("c.txt") as f:
    f.readline()
    print(f.readline().strip())
questions.hint: Each readline() call carries on from where the previous one stopped.
optionFeedback: red was read by the first readline(), which isn't printed.
Only the second readline() is printed, and it is one line.
Right: the second line is green.
Only two lines are read, so blue is never reached.

questions.explanation: The file has three lines, so the loop runs three times.
questions.code:
with open("d.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("x\ny\nz\n")
count = 0
with open("d.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        count += 1
print(count)
questions.hint: Work out what one step of a for loop over a file gives you.
optionFeedback: The loop counts lines, not characters.
The loop doesn't read the whole file at once; it goes line by line.
The file was written first, so it has lines to count.
Right: one step per line.

questions.prompt: Why are there blank lines between the names?
options: for loops can't read files properly
Each line still ends with \n, so print adds a second new line
questions.explanation: Each line keeps its \n; print() adds another. Print line.strip() instead.
questions.code:
with open("p.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Asha\nRavi\n")
with open("p.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line)
questions.hint: Think about what is at the very end of every line read from the file.
optionFeedback: The file is only read here, with the default "r" mode.
for loops are the normal way to read a file line by line.
write() only adds what you give it: here one \n after each name.
Right: strip() removes the extra new line.

questions.prompt: Which mode adds text to the end of a file without deleting what is there?
questions.hint: This mode was used in the log example to add more and end.
optionFeedback: Right: "a" appends.
"w" wipes the file first.
"r" is only for reading.
Modes are single letters, not words.

questions.explanation: Each line is turned into a number with int(), then added: 4 + 6 = 10.
questions.code:
with open("n.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("4\n6\n")
total = 0
with open("n.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        total += int(line.strip())
print(total)
questions.hint: Notice what int() does to each line before it is added to total.
optionFeedback: int() turns each line into a number, so they are added, not joined.
Right: 4 + 6 is 10.
Only total is printed, once, after the loop.
int() makes each line a number, and adding numbers is fine.

options: A for loop over a file gives one character at a time
A for loop over a file gives one line at a time, as text
readline() reads the whole file at once
Lines that look like numbers are read as numbers
questions.explanation: Looping over a file gives lines, and every line is a string.
questions.hint: Think about what the name line in for line in f actually holds.
optionFeedback: Looping over a file gives whole lines, not single characters.
Right: lines, and always strings.
read() reads everything; readline() reads one line.
Everything read from a file is text; use int() to get a number.

subLevels.title: Files that might not exist
subLevels.summary: Handle missing files with FileNotFoundError and os.path.exists().

blocks.text: Reading a file that doesn't exist raises FileNotFoundError. "w" and "a" create missing files, but "r" can't.

blocks.output: FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'missing.txt'
blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

items: Catch FileNotFoundError when a file might be missing.

blocks.code:
import os
print(os.path.exists("todo.txt"))
with open("todo.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("learn files\n")
print(os.path.exists("todo.txt"))
explanation: os.path.exists() gives True if the file is there and False if not.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Opening a file with "w" just to see if it exists. "w" creates an empty file and wipes any old text. To read safely, use "r" with try/except FileNotFoundError, or check os.path.exists() first.
Expect missing files: catch FileNotFoundError or check with os.path.exists() before reading.

blocks.title: In the app
blocks.text: In the Practical tab every run starts with an empty scratch folder, so a file is always missing until your program writes it.

questions.prompt: Which error does this code cause?
questions.explanation: Opening a file for reading when it doesn't exist raises FileNotFoundError.
questions.hint: Think about which mode open() uses by default and whether the file is there.
optionFeedback: open and f are fine names; it is the file that is missing.
KeyError is for dictionaries; this is a file.
Right: the file isn't there to read.
The file name is a valid string; the file just doesn't exist.

questions.explanation: x.txt was never created, so open() fails and the except block prints missing.
questions.hint: Every run starts with an empty folder, so check whether x.txt was ever written.
optionFeedback: Right: the file doesn't exist, so except runs.
open() fails first, so print("found") never runs.
The error happens before the found line, so only one message prints.
Neither print shows the file name.

questions.explanation: "a" creates the file when it is missing, so it exists afterwards.
questions.code:
import os
with open("new.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("hi")
print(os.path.exists("new.txt"))
questions.hint: Remember which modes create a file when it doesn't exist yet.
optionFeedback: "a" creates a missing file, so it exists now.
os.path.exists() answers True or False; it doesn't read the file.
Only reading a missing file fails; "a" creates it.
Right: "a" created the file.

options: Opening a file with "w" creates it if missing and wipes it if it exists
"r" mode creates the file if it is missing
FileNotFoundError can only happen in "w" mode
questions.explanation: "w" always gives you an empty file, which is why it is a bad way to check for a file.
questions.hint: Think about why the lesson warns against using this mode just to check for a file.
optionFeedback: Right: that is why "w" is risky for checking.
"r" raises FileNotFoundError when the file is missing.
os.path.exists() only looks; it never changes anything.
Missing files cause the error when reading, because "w" creates them.

questions.prompt: In the Practical tab, what happens to files your program writes?
options: They are kept in your phone's Downloads folder
They are deleted when the run ends, so read them in the same program
They are uploaded to the internet
The next program you run can read them
questions.explanation: The scratch folder is emptied after every run, so files only last while your program runs.
questions.hint: Recall the In the app tips about the scratch folder in this level.
optionFeedback: Files stay in the app's private scratch folder; other folders are blocked.
Right: the scratch folder is emptied after each run.
PyPath works offline and never uploads your files.
Each run starts with an empty scratch folder.

cheatSheet.title: Working with Files

items.code:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("hello\n")
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

items.note: "a" adds to the end and creates the file if missing.

items.code:
with open("n.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("4\n6\n")
total = 0
with open("n.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        total += int(line.strip())
print(total)
items.note: Loop over lines; strip() and convert them.

remember: Files hold text: use str() to write numbers and int() after reading.
In the Practical tab, files are deleted when the run ends.
